title: Look At 'Em
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. passes on a small practice from teacher Drew Campbell for the times when it is hard to like a student: simply look at the student's face for twenty or thirty seconds, a few times an hour, while they work on a warm-up or talk with others. Stuart wonders whether research backs the idea and points to the mere exposure effect, in which repeated exposure to a stimulus raises positive feeling toward it. He notes that the effect depends on the absence of aversive events, so the looking should happen when a student is doing something harmless or productive and not while disrupting the room. He has tried it during warm-ups and reports that noticing a student's concentration or effort does bring more warmth. The post is brief and offered as a low-cost relational habit for the tiring months of the fall.
points: Deliberately looking at a student for a few seconds at a time can raise a teacher's warmth toward a student they struggle to like.
The mere exposure effect offers research support, because repeated benign exposure to a face tends to increase liking.
The effect fails when exposure is paired with aversive events, so the practice works best while students are working quietly or productively.
Noticing specific evidence of effort, such as one student's concentration or another's earnest writing, gives the looking a concrete focus.
The habit echoes David Brooks' idea of the Illuminator, someone whose gaze is respectful, warm and admiring.
quotes: the thing to do when you’re struggling to like a student is just to look at their face for an extended amount of time. While they’re working on a warm-up or engaged in conversation, just sit and look at them.
What I often find, if I’m able to get away with doing this for twenty or thirty seconds a few times an hour, is that I’ll begin to like them more, just by looking at their face.
The idea is that simply being exposed to a stimulus (e.g., a student’s face) repeatedly increases positive affect for that stimulus.
If I’m looking at a student who is actively disrupting the learning environment, I’m unlikely to simply start liking the student more.
the time to look at a student for a bit of extra time is when they are doing something harmless (or, even better, something productive like working at learning).
During a warm-up, I’ll look out at the class and notice Brady’s concentration while he’s writing, or Ava’s earnest effort to get what’s on her mind onto the computer screen.
And I do tend to find that it brings just a bit more warmth into my heart for my students, even during the tired months of the fall in a classroom.
